q: Which statement about raising a pre-seed round is most accurate?
options: Most successful companies raise investment early, so it's the normal first step to take
Raising money is the clearest early sign that customers want what you're building
Many good companies never raise; customers' money, revenue and grants are real options
You should raise as much as you can while investors are still interested in your idea
why: Most companies never raise from investors, and most startups fail whether or not they raise. Customers paying you is a stronger sign of progress than investment.

q: You expect to spend $12,000 a month, your milestone is about 12 months away, and you want a six-month buffer. Roughly how much should your plan say you need?
why: Twelve months to the milestone plus a six-month buffer is 18 months, and 18 × $12,000 = $216,000. The buffer covers delays and the time it may take to raise again or reach profitability.

q: An angel puts $30,000 into a post-money SAFE (a US practice) with a $3 million valuation cap. Later, new investors buy 25% of the company in a priced round above the cap. Ignoring option pools, roughly what does the angel own afterward?
why: Before the round the angel owns $30,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 1%. The new investors take 25%, so every existing holder keeps 75% of their share, and 1% becomes 0.75%.

q: After a first meeting, an investor says they love your company and want to stay in touch. What should you do next?
options: Send a short thank-you with anything you promised, and keep talking to other investors
Stop contacting other investors so this one doesn't think you're being disloyal to them
Start hiring as if the money had arrived, so you don't lose valuable time
Wait quietly for them to send documents, so you don't come across as too eager or pushy
why: Enthusiasm in a meeting isn't a commitment. A prompt follow-up keeps the conversation going, and your other conversations protect you if this one doesn't turn into an investment.

q: Which of these is a red flag when someone offers to invest?
options: They ask to speak with two of your customers before making a decision
They want you to sign within 24 hours, without a lawyer reviewing it
They ask to see your monthly numbers for the last six months
They say they need two weeks to talk it over with their partners first
why: Speaking to customers, checking numbers and taking time to decide are all normal. Pressure to sign quickly without legal review is a warning sign, whatever the terms say.
